explainer.subject: Mathematics
explainer.title: Why the inside needs its own derivative

steps.say: To differentiate $\sin(x^2)$, it feels natural to just change the sine to cosine and keep the $x^2$ the same.
If $x$ changes by a little, $x^2$ changes by about $2x$ times as much. The rate of change of the whole function must account for this 'inner speed'.
Think of it as two linked gears: the outer gear (sine) is being turned by an inner gear ($x^2$). The final speed depends on both.
The Chain Rule states we multiply the derivative of the outer layer by the derivative of the inner layer.
We take the derivative of the sine part first, then multiply by the derivative of the inner $x^2$ part.
Before moving on, identify the 'inside' part and verify its derivative is multiplied at the end.

explainer.takeaway: To differentiate a nested function, always multiply by the 'inner speed'—the derivative of the inside part.
